In 1995, Cameron co-produced [*Strange Days*](/wiki/Strange_Days_(film) "Strange Days (film)"), a science fiction thriller. Directed by Kathryn Bigelow and co-written by [Jay Cocks](/wiki/Jay_Cocks "Jay Cocks"), *Strange Days* was critically and financially unsuccessful.[[48]](#cite_note-48) In 1996, Cameron reunited with the cast of *Terminator 2* to film *[T2 3-D: Battle Across Time](/wiki/T2_3-D:_Battle_Across_Time "T2 3-D: Battle Across Time")*, an attraction at [Universal Studios Florida](/wiki/Universal_Studios_Florida "Universal Studios Florida"), and in other parks around the world.[[49]](#cite_note-49)

His next major project was [*Titanic*](/wiki/Titanic_(1997_film) "Titanic (1997 film)") (1997), an [epic](/wiki/Epic_film "Epic film") about the [RMS *Titanic*](/wiki/Titanic "Titanic"), which [sank](/wiki/Sinking_of_the_Titanic "Sinking of the Titanic") in 1912 after hitting an iceberg. With a production budget of $200 million, at the time it was the [most expensive film ever made](/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_films "List of most expensive films"). Starting in 1995, Cameron took several dives to the bottom of the [Atlantic Ocean](/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") to capture footage of the [wreck](/wiki/Wreck_of_the_Titanic "Wreck of the Titanic"), which would later be used in the film.[[50]](#cite_note-50) A replica of the ship was built in [Rosarito Beach](/wiki/Rosarito_Beach "Rosarito Beach") and [principal photography](/wiki/Principal_photography "Principal photography") began in September 1996. *Titanic* made headlines before its release, for being over-budget and exceeding its schedule.[[51]](#cite_note-51)[[52]](#cite_note-52) In a radical departure from Cameron's previous work, his completed screenplay depicts two [star-crossed](/wiki/Star-crossed "Star-crossed") lovers, portrayed by [Leonardo DiCaprio](/wiki/Leonardo_DiCaprio "Leonardo DiCaprio") and [Kate Winslet](/wiki/Kate_Winslet "Kate Winslet"), from different social classes who fall in love amid the backdrop of the ship's tragedy. The supporting cast includes [Billy Zane](/wiki/Billy_Zane "Billy Zane")

The role of [president of the Security Council](/wiki/President_of_the_United_Nations_Security_Council "President of the United Nations Security Council") involves setting the agenda, presiding at its meetings and overseeing any crisis. The president is authorized to issue both [presidential statements](/wiki/Presidential_Statement "Presidential Statement") (subject to consensus amongst Council members) and notes,[[95]](#cite_note-99)[[96]](#cite_note-un.org-100) which are used to make declarations of intent that the full Security Council can then pursue.[[96]](#cite_note-un.org-100) The presidency of the council is held by each of the members in turn for one month, following the English alphabetical order of the member states' names.[[97]](#cite_note-101) No distinction is made between permanent and non-permanent members in the rotation.

The design of the Eiffel Tower is attributed to [Maurice Koechlin](/wiki/Maurice_Koechlin "Maurice Koechlin") and [Émile Nouguier](/wiki/%C3%89mile_Nouguier "Émile Nouguier"), two senior engineers working for the [Compagnie des Établissements Eiffel](/wiki/Gustave_Eiffel "Gustave Eiffel"). It was envisaged after discussion about a suitable centrepiece for the proposed [1889 Exposition Universelle](/wiki/Exposition_Universelle_(1889) "Exposition Universelle (1889)"), a [world's fair](/wiki/World%27s_fair "World's fair") to celebrate the centennial of the [French Revolution](/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"). In May 1884, working at home, Koechlin made a sketch of their idea, described by him as "a great pylon, consisting of four lattice girders standing apart at the base and coming together at the top, joined together by metal [trusses](/wiki/Truss "Truss") at regular intervals".[[10]](#cite_note-10) Eiffel initially showed little enthusiasm, but he did approve further study, and the two engineers then asked [Stephen Sauvestre](/wiki/Stephen_Sauvestre "Stephen Sauvestre"), the head of the company's architectural department, to contribute to the design. Sauvestre added decorative arches to the base of the tower, a glass pavilion to the first level, and other embellishments.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/53/Maurice_koechlin_pylone.jpg/250px-Maurice_koechlin_pylone.jpg)](/wiki/File:Maurice_koechlin_pylone.jpg)

Imbens received the 2021 [Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences](/wiki/Nobel_Memorial_Prize_in_Economic_Sciences "Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences") along with fellow economists [David Card](/wiki/David_Card "David Card") and Joshua Angrist for their contributions toward methodologies for the analysis of [causal relationships](/wiki/Causal_relation "Causal relation").[[30]](#cite_note-30) In its press release, the [Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences](/wiki/Royal_Swedish_Academy_of_Sciences "Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences") stated that they "have provided us with new insights about the labour market and shown what conclusions about cause and effect can be drawn from natural experiments. Imbens has been married to fellow economist [Susan Athey](/wiki/Susan_Athey "Susan Athey") since 2002.[[32]](#cite_note-32) Athey likewise teaches at the Stanford Graduate School of Business where she holds the Economics of Technology Professorship.[[33]](#cite_note-33) The best man at Imbens and Athey's wedding was [Joshua Angrist](/wiki/Joshua_Angrist "Joshua Angrist"), with whom Imbens would share the Nobel prize 19 years later.[[34]](#cite_note-34)
